title: Levels of organization and the cell
blurb: Put the six levels of body organization in order and classify any structure as a molecule, cell, tissue, organ or organ system.
question: A biology instructor holds up a model of the stomach and asks the class to name its level of organization, then the level of the smooth muscle layer inside it. What are the two answers, and how do you tell them apart?

teach.body: The body is organized in six levels, each built from the one below: chemical (atoms and molecules), cellular, tissue, organ, organ system and organism. Plain English: atoms build molecules, molecules build cells, similar cells build tissues, different tissues build organs, related organs build systems, and all the systems together make one living person.

teach.caption: Read it bottom to top for smallest to largest. Every level contains all of the levels beneath it.

teach.h: The cell is the smallest living unit
teach.body: Atoms and molecules are essential, but they are not alive on their own. Cell theory states that the cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life and that all cells come from pre-existing cells. So the chemical level is the smallest level, while the cellular level is the smallest level that is alive. Each step up adds abilities the level below does not have alone.

teach.h: Tissue versus organ: the line the exam tests
teach.body: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together on a common function. An organ is a structure made of two or more tissue types working together. The stomach is an organ because it contains all four tissue types: epithelial lining, connective tissue, smooth muscle and nerves. Blood is a tissue (connective tissue with a fluid matrix), and the heart is an organ.

teach.h: Why the stomach counts as an organ
teach.caption: One tissue type alone is still only a tissue. Two or more working together make an organ.
Skin is the largest organ in the body by area and weight.

head: Organ system
Example organs
teach.caption: Each system has its own HESI A2 objective; here you only need to sort organs into the right system.

teach.h: Scenario: Keisha reads a lab slide
teach.body: Keisha, a pre-nursing student, views a slide of the stomach wall. One layer is a sheet of columnar cells: that sheet is a tissue (epithelial). Under it sits a band of smooth muscle cells: another tissue. The stomach containing both, plus connective and nervous tissue, is an organ. The stomach, liver and intestines working together form the digestive system, an organ system.

teach.text: Three classic slips: calling blood an organ (it is a connective tissue); listing the cellular level as smallest (the chemical level is smaller, but the cell is the smallest LIVING level); and defining an organ system as a group of tissues (it is a group of organs).

items: Order: chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
The cell is the smallest unit of life; atoms and molecules are not alive.
Tissue = similar cells with a shared function; organ = two or more tissue types.
Blood is a connective tissue; the heart, kidney and skin are organs.
An organ system is a group of organs, such as the digestive system.

summary: You can now list the six levels of organization in order from chemical to organism and explain why the cell is the smallest living level. You can also tell a tissue from an organ and sort common organs into their organ systems.

A.q: Which sequence lists levels of organization from smallest to largest?
options: Cellular, chemical, tissue, organ, organ system
Chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, organ system
Chemical, tissue, cellular, organ, organ system
Chemical, cellular, organ, tissue, organ system
A.why: Atoms and molecules (chemical) build cells, similar cells build tissues, tissues build organs, and organs build organ systems.

whyNot.0: The chemical level is smaller than the cellular level: cells are made of molecules.
whyNot.2: Tissues are made of cells, so the cellular level must come before the tissue level.
whyNot.3: Organs are made of tissues, so the tissue level must come before the organ level.

A.q: Which structure is an example of the tissue level of organization?
A.why: Blood is a connective tissue: cells suspended in a fluid matrix (plasma), all working together on transport.

whyNot.1: The heart contains several tissue types working together, so it is an organ.
whyNot.2: One neuron is a single cell, so it belongs to the cellular level.
whyNot.3: The spleen is built from more than one tissue type, so it is an organ of the lymphatic system.

A.q: What is the smallest level of organization that is considered alive?
A.why: Cell theory: the cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life. Nothing smaller is alive on its own.

whyNot.0: The chemical level is smaller, but atoms and molecules are not alive by themselves.
whyNot.1: Tissues are alive, but they are made of cells, so they are not the smallest living level.
whyNot.2: Organs are alive, but they sit two levels above the cell.

B.q: A structure made of two or more tissue types that work together to perform a specific function is
B.why: That is the definition of an organ, such as the stomach, which contains all four tissue types.

whyNot.1: A tissue is a group of similar cells, not a combination of different tissue types.
whyNot.2: An organ system is a group of related organs, one level above an organ.
whyNot.3: An organism is the whole living individual made of all the organ systems.

B.q: Which statement BEST explains why the stomach is classified as an organ?
options: It is made of one specialized cell type
It works with the liver to digest food
It is lined by a single layer of cells
It combines two or more tissue types
B.why: An organ is defined by containing two or more tissue types working together; the stomach has epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue.

whyNot.0: A structure made of one cell type would be a tissue at most, not an organ.
whyNot.1: Working with other organs describes membership of an organ system, not what makes it an organ.
whyNot.2: A single layer of cells describes simple epithelium, which is a tissue.

B.q: Which pairing of structure and level of organization is CORRECT?
B.why: The kidney is built from several tissue types working together, so it is an organ.

whyNot.0: A molecule such as glucose belongs to the chemical level.
whyNot.1: Adipose is a connective tissue, so it belongs to the tissue level.
whyNot.3: The urinary system is a group of organs, so it is an organ system, one level below the organism.

C.q: Under a microscope, Priya sees a sheet of similar flat cells stacked in several layers, all working together to protect an underlying surface. Which level of organization does this sheet represent?
C.why: Many similar cells working together on one function form a tissue; here, a stratified squamous epithelium.

whyNot.0: The cellular level would be one cell; she is looking at many similar cells acting as a unit.
whyNot.1: An organ needs two or more different tissue types; this sheet is one type of tissue.
whyNot.3: An organ system is a group of organs, far larger than one sheet of cells.

C.q: Which statement about levels of organization is INCORRECT?
options: Each organ contains two or more tissue types
An organ system is a group of related tissues
Blood is classified as a type of connective tissue
Atoms and molecules form the chemical level
C.why: An organ system is a group of related ORGANS (for example, the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra), not a group of tissues.

whyNot.0: This is correct: two or more tissue types working together is what defines an organ.
whyNot.2: This is correct: blood is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix called plasma.
whyNot.3: This is correct: the chemical level is made of atoms and the molecules they form.

C.q: Andre writes this sequence in order of increasing complexity: protein molecule, ____, cardiac muscle tissue, heart, cardiovascular system. What belongs in the blank?
C.why: The cellular level sits between the chemical level (protein molecule) and the tissue level (cardiac muscle tissue), so the blank is a cardiac muscle cell.

whyNot.0: A coronary artery is a blood vessel built from several tissues, so it is at the organ level, not between molecule and tissue.
whyNot.2: The myocardium is the heart's muscle layer, made of cardiac muscle tissue, so it is not the cellular level.
whyNot.3: Plasma is the fluid matrix of blood; it is part of a tissue, not the cellular level.

reteach.title: Think of the body as a book
reteach.question: A book is built from letters, words, sentences, paragraphs and chapters. If the body were a book, which part would match each level of organization?

blocks.h: Letters up to the whole book
blocks.body: Letters are like atoms and molecules: needed everywhere but meaningless alone. A word is the smallest unit that carries meaning, just as a cell is the smallest unit that is alive. Words form sentences (tissues), sentences form paragraphs (organs), paragraphs form chapters (organ systems), and the chapters together make the book (the organism).

blocks.text: A paragraph needs more than one sentence, just as an organ needs more than one tissue type. That is why blood (one tissue) is not an organ but the heart is.

explain.body: Chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. Each level is built from the one directly below it.

test.q: Which level of organization comes immediately after the cellular level?
test.why: Similar cells working together form tissues, so tissue is the next level up from cellular.

whyNot.0: The chemical level comes before the cellular level, not after it.
whyNot.1: The organ level comes after tissue, so it skips a level.
whyNot.2: The organ system level comes after organ, two steps beyond tissue.

explain.body: Atoms and molecules (water, proteins, glucose) make up the chemical level. They are not alive. The cell is the smallest unit that is alive.

test.q: A water molecule inside a muscle cell belongs to which level of organization?
test.why: Molecules such as water belong to the chemical level, wherever they happen to be.

whyNot.1: Being inside a cell does not make a molecule part of the cellular level; the cell itself is.
whyNot.2: Tissue is made of many cells, two levels above a molecule.
whyNot.3: The organism is the whole person, the highest level.

explain.body: Tissue = similar cells with a common function (blood, adipose, cartilage). Organ = two or more tissue types working together (heart, kidney, skin, stomach).

test.q: Which of these is an organ rather than a tissue?
test.why: Skin contains epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue working together, and it is the largest organ in the body.

whyNot.0: Adipose (fat) is a single type of connective tissue.
whyNot.1: Cartilage is a single type of connective tissue.
whyNot.3: Blood is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix, not an organ.

explain.body: Related organs form an organ system. There are 11: integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic/immune, respiratory, digestive, urinary and reproductive.

test.q: The lymph nodes and the spleen belong to which organ system?
test.why: Lymph nodes and the spleen are lymphoid organs of the lymphatic (immune) system.

whyNot.0: The spleen filters blood, but it is a lymphoid organ, not part of the cardiovascular system of heart and vessels.
whyNot.2: The spleen sits near the stomach, but it does not digest food.
whyNot.3: Neither lymph nodes nor the spleen is classed as an endocrine gland.
